claims.statement: Semax (ACTH4-7-PGP) is a synthetic heptapeptide with sequence Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro, molecular formula C37H51N9O10S, molecular weight approximately 813.9, CAS number 80714-61-0, indexed in PubChem as CID 9811102 under the name 'ACTH (4-7), Pro-Gly-Pro-'.

context.formulation: synthetic peptide, reference/research and Russian pharmaceutical (Peptogen) forms

reviewFlags: DrugBank/ChEMBL identifiers not resolved this session

claims.statement: Semax's mechanism of action is not established; it is proposed to interact with melanocortin receptors or inhibit enkephalinase enzymes based on its structural relationship to ACTH(4-10), but this is not confirmed as a defined human pharmacological mechanism.

extractedEvidence.quote: The mechanism of action of Semax is unknown.
might interact with certain melanocortin receptors or inhibit enkephalinase enzymes

reviewFlags: sourced from a tertiary (encyclopedia) reference; primary mechanistic literature (largely rodent) not independently re-verified this session because PMC pages returned reCAPTCHA challenges instead of content
do not extrapolate proposed mechanism into a human efficacy claim

claims.statement: In Russia, Semax nasal drops (manufactured by Peptogen) are labeled with indications including intellectual/mnestic (memory, attention) disorders and post-traumatic-brain-injury/neurosurgery/narcosis states (0.1% formulation, including use as a nootropic in children from age 7 for minimal brain dysfunction including ADHD), and the acute period of moderate-to-severe ischemic stroke as part of complex therapy (1% formulation). Semax is not FDA-approved and has no approved indication in the United States.

context.population: patients in Russia per product labeling; children 7+ for the 0.1% pediatric nootropic indication
context.useCase: Russian-labeled indications: cognitive/memory disorders, post-TBI/neurosurgery states, pediatric minimal brain dysfunction/ADHD, acute ischemic stroke

reviewFlags: foreign (Russian) product label, not an FDA-approved label; approval status and label text should be reconfirmed against the current official Russian State Register of Medicines at review time

claims.statement: Semax (heptapeptide) was nominated for inclusion on FDA's 503A bulk drug substances Category 2 list (substances that may present significant safety risks, flagged for immunogenicity risk from aggregation or peptide-related impurities) but the nomination was withdrawn by the nominator; it is listed on FDA's page under 'bulk drug substances nominated but withdrawn' rather than as an active Category 2 safety-risk substance. Semax has no FDA-approved drug application and is not on FDA's positive 503A Bulks List.

context.population: US-based compounding pharmacies and patients receiving compounded products

extractedEvidence.quote: Compounded drugs containing semax (heptapeptide) may pose risk for immunogenicity for certain routes of administration due to the potential for aggregation and peptide-related impurities.

reviewFlags: verify current status against the live FDA bulk-substances page at review time, since Category 2 and withdrawn-nomination listings have been revised in past cycles (e.g. April 2026 peptide-listing revisions noted for other compounds)

claims.statement: Per the Russian Semax product label, the drug is contraindicated in hypersensitivity to its components, in children under 7 years old (under 18 for ophthalmic/neurosurgical use), in pregnancy and lactation (no clinical studies conducted in these populations), in acute psychotic states or disorders accompanied by anxiety, and in patients with a history of seizures/cramps. Prolonged use may cause mild nasal mucosa irritation.

claims.statement: A 2018 meta-analysis of Russian clinical literature identified 8 studies (n=654) on intranasal Semax 1% (12-18 mg/day) given within 10-14 days of acute ischemic stroke onset, of which 3 studies (n=181) met inclusion criteria for pooled analysis; pooled results reported reduced stroke severity (NIHSS) at 10-14 and 21 days and improved Rivermead mobility scores versus comparators in moderate/severe stroke subgroups, with the study authors themselves calling for a rigorous multicenter double-blind trial to confirm the finding - indicating the underlying studies were not uniformly double-blind, placebo-controlled trials by modern standards.

context.population: adult ischemic stroke patients, primarily from Russian-language clinical literature
context.useCase: acute ischemic stroke, adjunct to standard therapy (investigational/label context, not a use recommendation)
context.doseText: 1% intranasal, 12-18 mg/day, administered within the first 10-14 days post-stroke (trial/label protocol context; not a use recommendation)

extractedEvidence.quote: significant stroke severity decrease reduction using NIHSS at 10-14 and 21 days
Semax 1% intranasal administration in the acute period of stroke leads to neurological impairment decrease, mobility and functional independence increase

reviewFlags: underlying evidence base is Russian-language, largely open-label clinical studies; no internationally replicated double-blind placebo-controlled RCT was located this session
trial/label dose context must never be presented as a use recommendation
does not establish efficacy for any indication other than acute ischemic stroke under medical supervision

claims.statement: Semax is widely marketed in the US gray/research-chemical market as a general cognitive-enhancement, focus, mood, and neuroprotective 'nootropic' for healthy adults, extrapolating from stroke-neuroprotection data and animal BDNF/long-term-potentiation findings; no controlled human trial in healthy (non-stroke) populations supporting these broader cognitive-enhancement claims was located, and vendor product pages simultaneously carry 'research use only, not for human consumption' disclaimers while marketing health-related benefit language.

context.population: consumers of gray-market Semax products marketed for cognitive enhancement
context.formulation: research-grade Semax nasal sprays/vials sold outside Russian pharmaceutical channels
context.useCase: nootropic / cognitive-enhancement / focus / mood marketing claims in healthy adults

extractedEvidence.quote: The strongest clinical evidence is in ischemic stroke neuroprotection; extrapolation to healthy cognitive enhancement is mechanistically reasonable but not directly established.
This product is intended strictly for laboratory research purposes. Not for human consumption, clinical use, veterinary applications, or any diagnostic or therapeutic purposes.

reviewFlags: misinformation-adjacent: popular nootropic/cognitive-enhancement marketing claims for healthy-adult use lack direct supporting human outcome evidence
stroke-specific efficacy data (limited, non-blinded) must not be generalized to healthy-population cognitive-enhancement claims

conflicts.summary: Semax holds Russian pharmaceutical labeling and marketing approval for stroke and cognitive indications, and a Russian meta-analysis reports positive pooled outcomes, but the underlying human studies are Russian-language and largely open-label rather than international double-blind placebo-controlled RCTs; no independent international regulator (FDA, EMA) has evaluated or approved Semax, and the meta-analysis authors themselves called for a more rigorous trial. The strength of the regulatory/marketing claim in Russia should not be read as equivalent to Strong-tier international efficacy evidence.

reviewReasons: Expansion-batch evidence packet requires human review before publication.

No internationally indexed, PMC/PubMed-verified double-blind placebo-controlled human RCT for Semax was located this session; PMC and PubMed article pages returned reCAPTCHA challenge pages instead of content on repeated attempts, so mechanism and trial-level primary literature could not be independently re-verified beyond the meta-analysis abstract and label.
RxNorm, UNII, DrugBank, and ChEMBL identifiers not resolved from structured databases this session.
Confirm current FDA bulk-substances withdrawn-nomination status for Semax against the live FDA page at review time, since peptide listings have been revised in recent cycles.
